stories.canonicalTitle: Kojiki, Part 5: Yamato Takeru
stories.editorialNote: 依据张伯伦 1882 年英译《古事记》第七十九至九十节（景行天皇纪第四至十五部分，sacred-texts 页码 kj086–kj097），按节顺序讲述；书中的歌只讲大意，不转录译文。故事开头小碓命杀兄的情节照原书交代结果，不渲染细节。《日本书纪》中的倭建命故事有不少不同之处，另行处理。

series.gapNote: 与上一部之间跳过第四十四至七十八节：神武天皇东征以及此后诸代天皇的记事，直到景行天皇纪的前三部分。

stories.summaryEn: Keikō's son Wo-usu is so fierce that his father fears him and sends him west against the Kumaso bravoes. Disguised as a girl in his aunt Yamato-hime's robes, he kills the two brothers at their feast, and the dying younger brother gives him the name Yamato Takeru. He kills the Izumo bravo with a wooden-sword trick, returns, and is at once sent east. At Ise he weeps to his aunt that his father wishes him dead; she gives him the Kusanagi sword and a bag. On the moor of Sagamu he mows the grass and lights a counter-fire to escape the flames; at sea Oto-tachibana-hime gives herself to the waves to calm them. On the Ashigara pass he sighs 'Alas, my wife!', and at Sakaori he finishes a poem with an old fire-keeper. Back in Owari he marries Miyazu-hime but leaves the sword with her and goes bare-handed against the deity of Mount Ibuki, who strikes him with hail. Sick, he walks on singing, dies at Nobo singing of his longing for Yamato, and turns into a white bird that flies into the sky.
stories.summaryZh: 景行天皇的儿子小碓命性情凶猛，父亲害怕他，就派他去西方讨伐熊曾建。他借来姑母倭比卖的衣裳，扮成少女混进宴会，刺杀了熊曾兄弟，垂死的弟弟献给他“倭建”的名号。他在出云用木刀骗杀了出云建，回到京城，父亲又立刻派他去东方。他在伊势向姑母哭诉父亲想让他死，姑母给了他草薙剑和一个袋子。在相武的原野上，他用剑割草、用袋中的火石点起逆火，逃出火海；渡海时弟橘比卖投身海中平息风浪。他在足柄坂上叹息“吾妻哉”，在酒折宫与火守老人联句。回到尾张，他娶了美夜受比卖，却把草薙剑留在她身边，空手去讨伐伊吹山的神，被冰雹击伤。他拖着病体一路走一路唱，在能烦野唱着思念故乡大和的歌死去，化作一只白鸟飞向天空。
stories.titleZh: 古事记 · 第五部 倭建命

claims.statement: Kojiki Section LXXIX says that when Keikō asked Wo-usu to teach his elder brother Oho-usu to come to meals, Wo-usu killed his brother, and the sovereign was afraid of his son's fierce heart.

Kojiki Section LXXX says Wo-usu, sent west against the Kumaso bravoes, took his aunt Yamato-hime's robe and skirt, let down his hair like a girl's and entered their housewarming feast, where they seated him between them.
Kojiki Section LXXX says Wo-usu killed both Kumaso bravoes at their feast, and that the dying younger brother, saying there was a braver man in Yamato than they, gave him the name Yamato Takeru.
Kojiki Section LXXXI says Yamato Takeru befriended the Izumo bravo, made a false wooden sword, exchanged swords with him after bathing in the river Hi, and killed him when he could not draw it.

Kojiki Section LXXXII says that when Yamato Takeru, sent east at once without troops, wept at Ise that his father wished him dead, his aunt Yamato-hime gave him the Kusanagi sword and a bag to open in an emergency.

Kojiki Section LXXXIII says that when the ruler of Sagamu set fire to the moor around him, Yamato Takeru opened his aunt's bag, mowed the grass with his sword and lit a counter-fire with the fire-striker, then killed the rulers, so that the place is called Yaizu.

Kojiki Section LXXXIV says that when the deity of the Hashirimizu strait raised waves against the boat, Oto-tachibana-hime spread rugs on the waves and entered the sea in Yamato Takeru's stead, the waves calmed, and seven days later her comb drifted ashore.

Kojiki Section LXXXV says Yamato Takeru killed the deity of the Ashigara pass, which came as a white deer, with a wild chive, and on the pass sighed three times 'Azuma haya', so that the land is called Azuma.

Kojiki Section LXXXVI says that at the palace of Sakaori in Kai, when Yamato Takeru asked in verse how many nights had passed since Niibari and Tsukuba, an old fire-keeper answered nine nights and ten days, and was made ruler of the East.

Kojiki Sections LXXXVII–LXXXVIII say Yamato Takeru married Miyazu-hime, left the Kusanagi sword with her and went bare-handed against Mount Ibuki, where he took the deity in the form of a white boar for its messenger and was struck senseless by hail.

Kojiki Section LXXXIX says Yamato Takeru, weakened, named the Awakening Spring, Tagi and the Staff Slope, found his forgotten sword still under the pine of Cape Otsu, and at Mie said his legs were like a thrice-bent rice cake.

Kojiki Sections LXXXIX–XC say Yamato Takeru died at Nobo after singing of his longing for Yamato and of the sword left by the maiden's bed, and that he turned into a great white bird that flew towards the shore, stopped at Shiki and rose into the sky again.

events.summaryEn: The Heavenly Sovereign Keikō ruled from the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku.
events.summaryZh: 景行天皇在缠向的日代宫统治天下，他有许多儿子，其中有一对兄弟：哥哥叫大碓命，弟弟叫小碓命，也叫倭男具那命。

events.summaryEn: The sovereign said: 'In the west there are two Kumaso bravoes who will not submit and have no respect.
events.summaryZh: 天皇说：西方有两个熊曾建，他们不肯归顺，没有礼数，你去把他们杀了。

events.summaryEn: When the feast was at its height, Wo-usu drew the sword from his bosom, seized the elder Kumaso bravo by the collar and thrust the sword through his chest.
events.summaryZh: 宴会正热闹的时候，小碓命从怀里拔出短剑，抓住哥哥熊曾建的衣领，一剑刺穿了他的胸膛。

events.summaryEn: On his way back Yamato Takeru subdued the deities of the mountains, the rivers and the straits, and then went into Izumo intending to kill the Izumo bravo.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命回京的路上，把山神、河神和海峡之神一一平定，然后进入出云国，想要杀死出云建。
events.titleEn: The Izumo bravo and the wooden sword

events.summaryEn: No sooner had Yamato Takeru returned than the sovereign commanded him again: 'Go and subdue the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East.' He sent with him Mi-suki-tomo-mimi-take-hiko, ancestor of the Kibi lords, and gave him a holly-wood spear eight fathoms long.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命刚刚回来，天皇又命令他说：你去把东方十二道那些凶暴的神和不肯归顺的人平定了。

events.summaryEn: In Owari, Yamato Takeru entered the house of Miyazu-hime, ancestress of the rulers of Owari, and thought to marry her; then, deciding to marry her on his return, he pledged himself to her and went on east.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命到了尾张国，进了尾张国造的祖先美夜受比卖的家，本想娶她为妻，转念一想，等回来时再娶吧，就和她立下婚约，继续往东去了。
events.titleEn: The fire on the moor of Sagamu

events.summaryEn: From there Yamato Takeru crossed the sea of Hashirimizu.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命从那里出发，渡过走水海。

events.summaryEn: Yamato Takeru went on deep into the East, subdued all the savage Emishi, pacified the savage deities of the mountains and rivers, and set out to return.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命继续深入东方，把凶暴的虾夷人都平定了，又平定了山河间凶暴的神，然后踏上了回程。
events.titleEn: The white deer on the Ashigara pass

events.summaryEn: Crossing from the pass into Kai, Yamato Takeru stayed at the palace of Sakaori.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命越过足柄坂，进入甲斐国，住在酒折宫里。

events.summaryEn: From Kai Yamato Takeru crossed Shinano, subdued the deity of the Shinano pass, and came back to Owari, to Miyazu-hime's house, to keep his pledge.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命从甲斐越过科野，平定了科野坂的神，回到尾张，进了美夜受比卖的家，履行当初的约定。

events.summaryEn: Coming down the mountain, he rested by the clear spring of Tamakurabe and his mind cleared a little, so the spring is called the Awakening Spring.
events.summaryZh: 倭建命下了山，来到玉仓部的清泉边休息，神志稍稍清醒了一些，所以那眼泉被叫作居寤清水。
events.titleEn: Legs like a triple-bent rice cake

events.summaryEn: At the moor of Nobo, longing for his home, he sang: Yamato is the best of lands; the green mountains fold round it like a fence; Yamato, how lovely.
events.summaryZh: 到了能烦野，倭建命思念故乡，唱道：大和是国中最好的地方，层层叠叠的青山像垣墙一样环绕，大和啊，多么美好。
events.titleEn: The songs of home and the white bird

versions.labelEn: Kojiki, Chamberlain translation, Sections LXXIX–XC (long retelling)
versions.labelZh: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第七十九至九十节（长篇讲述）
versions.narrativeScope: 小碓命与兄长、少女装扮刺杀熊曾建、出云建与木刀、伊势的姑母与草薙剑、尾张之约、相武的野火、弟橘比卖投海、足柄坂的白鹿、酒折宫的火守老人、伊吹山的白猪、当艺野与三重的腿、化为白鸟
versions.rightsNote: 张伯伦 1882 年译本属公共领域；本站发布按节顺序的独立讲述，神名采用现代通行读法。

sections.bodyEn: The Heavenly Sovereign Keikō ruled from the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku. Among his many sons were two brothers: the elder, Oho-usu, and the younger, Wo-usu, also called Yamato-woguna. One day the sovereign said to Wo-usu: 'Why does your elder brother not come to the morning and evening meals? Go and teach him.' Five days passed and still the elder brother did not come. The sovereign asked: 'Why does your brother still not come? Have you not taught him?' Wo-usu said he had. 'How did you teach him?' Wo-usu answered that he had waited for his brother at dawn when he went to the privy, seized him, broken his limbs, wrapped him in matting and thrown him away. The text tells it bluntly; this retelling gives only the outcome. The sovereign was afraid of his son's fierce and violent heart. The boy would later be called Yamato Takeru, and his hero's story begins with his father's fear. An earlier part tells that the sovereign had sent Oho-usu to summon two maidens of Mino to court, and that Oho-usu took them for himself and sent other women under their names; the sovereign knew and was troubled.
sections.bodyZh: 景行天皇在缠向的日代宫统治天下，他有许多儿子，其中有一对兄弟：哥哥叫大碓命，弟弟叫小碓命，也叫倭男具那命。有一天，天皇对小碓命说：你哥哥为什么早晚都不来一起用膳？你去好好教导他。过了五天，大碓命还是没有来。天皇问小碓命：你哥哥怎么还不来？你是不是没有教导他？小碓命回答：我已经教导过了。天皇问：你是怎么教导的？小碓命说：清早他去厕所的时候，我等着把他抓住，折断了他的手脚，用草席包起来扔掉了。这段话在书中说得很直接，本篇只交代结果。天皇听了，对这个儿子凶猛暴烈的性情感到害怕。这位少年后来的名字叫倭建命，他的英雄故事，就从父亲的这份恐惧开始。书中在前面的部分还记了一件事：天皇曾派大碓命去美浓召两位少女进宫，大碓命却把她们据为己有，另找别的女子冒名献上；天皇心里明白，却一直闷闷不乐。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第七十九节。

sections.bodyEn: The sovereign said: 'In the west there are two Kumaso bravoes who will not submit and have no respect. Go and kill them,' and sent Wo-usu west. He was still young, his hair bound up at the forehead in a boy's knot. He begged from his aunt Yamato-hime her upper robe and skirt, hid a short sword in his bosom, and set out. At the Kumaso bravoes' house he found it surrounded by three rings of warriors; the brothers were building a new cave-dwelling for a housewarming feast, and the place was full of noise. Wo-usu walked about nearby, waiting for the day of the feast. When it came he let down his hair like a girl's, put on his aunt's robe and skirt, became in every way a young girl, mingled with the women and went into the dwelling. The two Kumaso bravoes were taken with the maiden at once, seated her between them, and feasted. Yamato-hime was the sovereign's sister, serving Amaterasu at Ise; Kumaso lay roughly in the south of present-day Kyushu. So a prince with a boy's hair-knot walked alone into his enemies' feast in his aunt's clothes.
sections.bodyZh: 天皇说：西方有两个熊曾建，他们不肯归顺，没有礼数，你去把他们杀了。就派小碓命去了西方。那时小碓命还很年轻，头发在额前束成少年的发髻。他向姑母倭比卖命讨来她的上衣和裙子，又把一把短剑藏在怀里，出发了。到了熊曾建的家，只见房子四周围着三重军士，熊曾兄弟正在新建一座石室，准备举行落成的宴会，到处都是人声。小碓命在附近转了转，等着宴会的日子。到了那一天，他把束起的头发放下来梳成少女的样子，穿上姑母的衣裙，完全变成了一个少女，混在女人们中间，走进了石室。熊曾建兄弟一眼看中了这个少女，就让她坐在两人中间，一起饮酒作乐。倭比卖命是天皇的妹妹，在伊势侍奉天照大神；熊曾大致在今天九州的南部。一个束着少年发髻的皇子，就这样穿着姑母的衣裳，独自走进了敌人的宴席。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十节。

sections.bodyEn: When the feast was at its height, Wo-usu drew the sword from his bosom, seized the elder Kumaso bravo by the collar and thrust the sword through his chest. The younger bravo fled in terror; Wo-usu pursued him to the foot of the steps of the dwelling, caught him from behind and thrust the sword into him. The younger bravo said: 'Do not move the sword. I have something to say.' Holding him down, Wo-usu listened. 'Who is your augustness?' 'I am the son of the Heavenly Sovereign Ōtarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, who dwells in the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku and rules the Land of the Eight Great Islands; my name is King Yamato-woguna. The sovereign heard that you two Kumaso bravoes would not submit and had no respect, and sent me to kill you.' The bravo said: 'It is true. In the west there are none so brave and strong as we two; but in great Yamato there is a man braver than we. I will offer you a name: henceforth be called the August Child Yamato Takeru.' When he had spoken, Wo-usu killed him. From then on he was called Yamato Takeru. Takeru here means brave: Yamato Takeru is the brave one of Yamato. The name he is best known by was a tribute from a dying enemy.
sections.bodyZh: 宴会正热闹的时候，小碓命从怀里拔出短剑，抓住哥哥熊曾建的衣领，一剑刺穿了他的胸膛。弟弟熊曾建吓得转身就逃，小碓命追到石室的台阶下，从背后抓住他，把剑刺了进去。弟弟熊曾建说：不要动这把剑，我有话要说。小碓命就按住他，听他说。熊曾建问：您是谁？小碓命说：我是统治大八岛国、住在缠向日代宫的大带日子淤斯吕和气天皇的儿子，名叫倭男具那王。天皇听说你们熊曾建两个不肯归顺、没有礼数，派我来杀你们。熊曾建说：确实是这样。在西方，没有比我们兄弟两个更勇猛强悍的人了；可是在大倭国，却有比我们更勇猛的男子。我要献给你一个名号：从今以后，你就叫倭建御子吧。说完，小碓命就把他杀了。从此，人们称他为倭建命。“建”在这里是勇猛的意思，“倭建”就是“大和的勇士”。他一生最有名的这个名字，竟是一位敌人临死前送给他的赞许。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十节。

sections.bodyEn: On his way back Yamato Takeru subdued the deities of the mountains, the rivers and the straits, and then went into Izumo intending to kill the Izumo bravo. First he made friends with him, and secretly made a false sword of ichii wood, which he wore. One day they bathed together in the river Hi. Yamato Takeru came out first, girded on the sword the Izumo bravo had taken off, and said: 'Let us exchange swords.' The Izumo bravo came out and girded on the wooden sword. 'Come,' said Yamato Takeru, 'let us cross swords.' Each drew; the Izumo bravo could not draw the wooden sword, and Yamato Takeru drew the real one and killed him. He sang a song whose sense is: the sword the Izumo bravo wore, its scabbard wound with creepers many times — fine to look at, but with no blade inside, alas. Having subdued the west, he returned to the capital and reported to the sovereign. Both deeds, the girl's disguise and the exchange of swords, were won by trickery. The same wooden-sword trick and the same song appear in the Nihon shoki in a different story, between two brothers of Izumo; the two books tell it each in their own way.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命回京的路上，把山神、河神和海峡之神一一平定，然后进入出云国，想要杀死出云建。他先和出云建结为朋友，又暗中用赤梼木做了一把假刀，佩在身上。有一天，两人一起在肥河里洗澡。倭建命先从河里出来，把出云建解下的刀佩在自己身上，说：我们来交换刀吧。出云建从河里出来，就佩上了倭建命的那把木刀。倭建命说：来，我们比比刀法吧。两人各自拔刀，出云建拔不出那把木刀，倭建命就拔出真刀，把出云建杀了。他唱了一首歌，大意是：出云建佩的那把刀，刀鞘上缠着一层又一层的藤蔓，看起来很好，里面却没有刀身，真是可怜啊。他平定了西方，回到京城，向天皇复命。这两件事，一靠扮成少女，一靠交换刀剑，都是用计取胜。同样的木刀计和同一首歌，在《日本书纪》里被放进另一个故事：出云的一对兄弟之间。两部书在这里各有各的讲法。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十一节。
sections.headingEn: The Izumo bravo and the wooden sword

sections.bodyEn: No sooner had Yamato Takeru returned than the sovereign commanded him again: 'Go and subdue the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East.' He sent with him Mi-suki-tomo-mimi-take-hiko, ancestor of the Kibi lords, and gave him a holly-wood spear eight fathoms long. On his way east Yamato Takeru went first to Ise, worshipped at the shrine, and said to his aunt Yamato-hime, who served there: 'Does the sovereign wish me dead? He sent me to strike the savage people of the west, and I have hardly come back before, without giving me any troops, he sends me to subdue the savage people of the twelve roads of the East. Thinking of this, I can only believe he wishes me to die.' He wept as he spoke. When he left, Yamato-hime gave him the Kusanagi sword — the sword Susanoo took from the serpent's tail and the August Grandchild brought down from heaven — and a bag, saying: 'If anything urgent happens, open the mouth of this bag.' The spear is called in the original an eight-fathom spear of hihiragi, the holly. What the bag held he did not yet know. A prince fresh from great deeds weeping before his aunt is one of the rare scenes in the Kojiki that show a hero's weakness.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命刚刚回来，天皇又命令他说：你去把东方十二道那些凶暴的神和不肯归顺的人平定了。天皇派吉备臣的祖先御锄友耳建日子跟他同行，又赐给他一支柊木做的八寻长矛。倭建命出发去东方，先到了伊势，参拜神宫，对在那里侍奉的姑母倭比卖命说：天皇是不是想让我死？他派我去打西方那些凶暴的人，我回来还没有多久，又不给我军队，就要派我去平定东方十二道的凶暴之人。这样想来，天皇一定是想让我死啊。他一边诉说，一边哭泣。临走时，倭比卖命把草薙剑交给他——这就是须佐之男从八岐大蛇尾中得到、天孙降临时带到人间的那把剑——又给了他一个袋子，说：如果遇到紧急的事情，就打开这个袋子。那支长矛，原文叫“比比罗木之八寻矛”，比比罗木就是柊树。至于袋子里装着什么，他当时并不知道。一个刚刚立下大功的皇子在姑母面前哭泣，这是《古事记》里少有的、写英雄软弱的一幕。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十二节。

sections.bodyEn: In Owari, Yamato Takeru entered the house of Miyazu-hime, ancestress of the rulers of Owari, and thought to marry her; then, deciding to marry her on his return, he pledged himself to her and went on east. He subdued the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the mountains and rivers one by one. In Sagamu the local ruler deceived him: 'In this moor is a great marsh, and the deity of the marsh is very violent.' Yamato Takeru went into the moor to see the deity, and the ruler set fire to the moor all round. Knowing he had been deceived, he opened his aunt's bag and found a fire-striker. First he mowed the grass around him with the Kusanagi sword, then lit a counter-fire with the striker and drove back the oncoming fire, and came out safe. He turned back, killed all those rulers and burned them, so that the place is still called Yaizu, Burning Ford. The Nihon shoki says the sword was named Kusanagi, Grass-Mower, from this deed; the Kojiki already calls it so in the earlier serpent story. The text places this in Sagamu, while the name Yaizu belongs today to Suruga, in Shizuoka — a discrepancy long discussed by commentators.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命到了尾张国，进了尾张国造的祖先美夜受比卖的家，本想娶她为妻，转念一想，等回来时再娶吧，就和她立下婚约，继续往东去了。他把山河间凶暴的神和不肯归顺的人一一平定。到了相武国，那里的国造骗他说：这片原野里有一个大沼泽，住在沼泽里的神非常凶暴。倭建命就走进原野去看那位神。国造在原野上四面放火。倭建命知道上了当，打开姑母给的袋子，里面是一块打火石。他先用草薙剑割开身边的草，再用打火石点起一圈逆火，把烧来的大火挡了回去，平安地走了出来。他回过头来，把那些国造全部杀死，放火烧掉，所以那个地方至今叫作烧津。《日本书纪》说这把剑因为割草而得名“草薙”，而《古事记》在更早的大蛇故事里就已经这样称呼它了。书中把这件事记在相武国，而“烧津”这个地名今天在骏河，也就是静冈县，这一点历来被注释家讨论。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十三节。
sections.headingEn: The fire on the moor of Sagamu

sections.bodyEn: From there Yamato Takeru crossed the sea of Hashirimizu. The deity of the strait raised great waves; the boat spun round and could not go forward. Then his consort Oto-tachibana-hime said: 'I will enter the sea in the prince's stead. The prince must accomplish the task he was sent on and report to the sovereign.' When she was about to enter the sea, she spread eight layers of sedge rugs, eight layers of skin rugs and eight layers of silk rugs on the waves, sat on them, and sank into the sea. The raging waves calmed of themselves and the boat could go on. Before she went she sang a song whose sense is: on the little moor of Sagamu among the standing peaks, in the midst of the burning fire, you stood and asked after me — ah, you. Seven days later her comb drifted ashore. Yamato Takeru took up the comb, made her a tomb and laid the comb in it. Her song shows that in the fire on the moor of Sagamu she had been at her husband's side. The Hashirimizu sea is roughly the Uraga channel at the mouth of Tokyo Bay, its current so swift that it was called Running Water.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命从那里出发，渡过走水海。海峡的神掀起大浪，船在原地打转，无法前进。这时，倭建命的妃子弟橘比卖命说：我代替皇子进入海中吧。皇子应当完成被派来做的事，回去向天皇复命。她要入海的时候，在浪上铺了八层菅草垫子、八层皮垫子和八层绸缎垫子，坐在上面，沉入了海中。汹涌的波浪自己平息下来，船又能前进了。弟橘比卖临走前唱了一首歌，大意是：在相武那群山耸立的小原野上，熊熊大火之中，你站在火里还在问我是否平安——啊，你啊。七天以后，她的梳子漂到了岸边。倭建命拾起那把梳子，为她修了陵墓，把梳子安放在里面。这首歌让人知道，在相武原野的大火里，她一直在丈夫的身边。走水海大致是今天东京湾口的浦贺水道一带，水流湍急，所以叫作“走水”。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十四节。

sections.bodyEn: Yamato Takeru went on deep into the East, subdued all the savage Emishi, pacified the savage deities of the mountains and rivers, and set out to return. At the foot of the Ashigara pass, as he was eating his dried rice, the deity of the pass changed into a white deer and came and stood before him. He took up the leftover end of the wild chive he had been eating, waited for the deer to come near, threw it, struck it in the eye and killed it. Then he climbed the pass, looked back the way he had come, remembered Oto-tachibana-hime who had sunk into the sea, and sighed three times: 'Azuma haya!' — 'Alas, my wife!' Therefore, says the text, the land has been called Azuma, the East. A sigh became the name of a land. Through all his fighting Yamato Takeru never complained; only here does he show his deep grief. The Emishi were the peoples of the East who did not submit to the court; the Ashigara pass lies in the mountains on the border of present-day Kanagawa and Shizuoka. The small detail of the wild chive striking the deer's eye makes the mountain deity's death all the more sudden.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命继续深入东方，把凶暴的虾夷人都平定了，又平定了山河间凶暴的神，然后踏上了回程。来到足柄坂下，他正在吃干粮，那座山坡的神变成一只白鹿，走过来站在他面前。倭建命拿起吃剩的野蒜，等白鹿走近时扔过去，正好打中了它的眼睛，把它打死了。他登上足柄坂，回望来路，想起沉入海中的弟橘比卖，长叹了三声：吾妻哉！——“啊，我的妻子！”所以，书中说，从此人们就把那片土地叫作“阿豆麻”，也就是“东国”。这一声叹息，成了一个地方的名字。倭建命一路征战，从不诉苦，只在这里流露了一次深深的悲伤。虾夷指当时东方不服从朝廷的人们；足柄坂在今天神奈川与静冈交界的山上。白鹿被野蒜打中眼睛，这样细小的一笔，让这位山神的死显得格外突然。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十五节。
sections.headingEn: The white deer on the Ashigara pass

sections.bodyEn: Crossing from the pass into Kai, Yamato Takeru stayed at the palace of Sakaori. One day he sang a line: since passing Niibari and Tsukuba, how many nights have I slept? — that is, how many nights since leaving Niibari and Tsukuba in the East? None of his followers could answer it. Then an old man who was tending the fire took it up: counting the days, of nights there have been nine, of days ten. Yamato Takeru praised the old man and made him ruler of the Eastern Land. This exchange of two lines has been seen in later times as one of the beginnings of linked verse in Japan. On the long campaign it is a rare quiet moment: a weary prince counting the days away from home, and a humble old man counting them for him. Niibari and Tsukuba are in present-day Ibaraki, Kai is present-day Yamanashi, and the site of Sakaori is in today's Kofu. None of his attendants could answer; it was the old man watching the fire who did.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命越过足柄坂，进入甲斐国，住在酒折宫里。有一天，他唱了一句歌：越过新治和筑波，已经睡了几夜？——意思是说，离开东方的新治与筑波以来，已经过了多少个夜晚了？身边的人没有一个能接下去。这时，一个在旁边看守火堆的老人接着唱道：数一数日子，夜是九夜，日是十日。倭建命十分赞赏这个老人，就封他为东国造。这一问一答的两句歌，后世被看作日本连歌的起源之一。在征战的长途中，这是少有的安静时刻：一位疲倦的皇子数着离家的日子，一位卑微的老人替他把日子数了出来。新治与筑波都在今天的茨城县，甲斐就是今天的山梨县，酒折宫的旧址在今天的甲府。身边的随从没有一个答得上来，答出这一句的，却是一个看火的老人。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十六节。

sections.bodyEn: From Kai Yamato Takeru crossed Shinano, subdued the deity of the Shinano pass, and came back to Owari, to Miyazu-hime's house, to keep his pledge. They exchanged songs and were married. Then he left the Kusanagi sword with Miyazu-hime and went bare-handed to take the deity of Mount Ibuki, saying: 'As for the deity of this mountain, I will take him with my bare hands.' Climbing the mountain, he met on its slope a white boar as big as an ox. He said aloud: 'This one that has turned into a white boar must be the messenger of the mountain deity. I will not kill it now; I will kill it on my way back,' and went on climbing. But the white boar was no messenger; it was the deity himself. Because of these boastful words the deity sent down a great storm of hail that struck Yamato Takeru senseless. The sword that had protected him all the way was no longer at his side. The text also tells that at the feast he saw the stain of her monthly blood on the hem of her robe and questioned her in song, and she answered in song that months had passed and the moon had risen while she waited for him. Mount Ibuki lies on the border of present-day Shiga and Gifu. Later commentators see his boastful speech against the deity — kotoage, speaking out — as what brought the disaster on him.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命从甲斐越过科野，平定了科野坂的神，回到尾张，进了美夜受比卖的家，履行当初的约定。两人以歌相答，结为夫妻。随后，他把草薙剑留在美夜受比卖的身边，空着手去讨伐伊服岐能山——伊吹山——的神，说：这座山的神，我空手就能把他抓住。他登上山去，在山坡上遇见一头白色的野猪，大得像一头牛。倭建命大声说：这头变成白猪的，是山神的使者吧。现在不杀它，等我回来的时候再杀。说完就继续往上走。可是那头白猪并不是使者，正是山神本人。因为他说了这样的大话，山神降下了猛烈的冰雹，打得倭建命神志昏迷。这把一路保护他的剑，此刻已经不在他的身边。书中还记下，宴会上倭建命看见她外衣的下摆沾着月事的血迹，便以歌相问，她以歌相答，说日月流转，等他等得月亮都已升起。伊吹山在今天滋贺与岐阜的交界处。后世注释家认为，倭建命对着山神口出狂言——原文称为“言举”——正是招来灾祸的原因。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十七至八十八节。

sections.bodyEn: Coming down the mountain, he rested by the clear spring of Tamakurabe and his mind cleared a little, so the spring is called the Awakening Spring. He went on to the moor of Tagi and said: 'My heart always longed to fly through the sky, but now my feet will not walk; they stagger.' So the place is called Tagi. Leaning on a staff he walked slowly on, and the slope is called the Staff Slope. At the single pine on Cape Otsu he found a sword he had left there once while eating, still lying where he had left it, and he sang: single pine of Cape Otsu, my elder brother — if you were a man, I would gird you with a sword and clothe you. At the village of Mie he said: 'My legs are like a rice cake bent three times; I am utterly weary.' So the place is called Mie. The text records the place-names he left behind, as if marking his ever heavier steps. Tagi lies in present-day Gifu and Cape Otsu near Kuwana in Ise; the name of Mie Prefecture is said to come from this place. The sword under the lone pine had been waiting all along for its master.
sections.bodyZh: 倭建命下了山，来到玉仓部的清泉边休息，神志稍稍清醒了一些，所以那眼泉被叫作居寤清水。他继续往前走，到了当艺野，说：我的心本来总想在天空中飞翔，可现在我的脚却走不动了，变得蹒跚踉跄。所以那里叫作当艺。他又拄着手杖慢慢地走，那段坡就叫杖衡坂。到了尾津岬的一棵孤松下，他发现以前在这里吃饭时忘下的一把刀，竟然还在原处。他唱道：尾津岬那棵孤松啊，我的兄长，你若是人，我就给你佩上刀，给你穿上衣服。到了三重村，他说：我的腿像三重弯曲的年糕一样，累极了。所以那里叫作三重。书中一路记下他留下的地名，像是记下了他越来越沉重的脚步。当艺在今天的岐阜一带，尾津岬在伊势的桑名附近，据说今天三重县的名字也与这里有关。那棵孤松下的刀，原来一直在等着它的主人。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十九节。
sections.headingEn: Legs like a triple-bent rice cake

sections.bodyEn: At the moor of Nobo, longing for his home, he sang: Yamato is the best of lands; the green mountains fold round it like a fence; Yamato, how lovely. And: let those whose lives are whole put leaves of the bear-oak of Mount Heguri in their hair. And: ah, the clouds rising from the direction of my home. When his sickness grew grave he sang a last song: by the maiden's bed I left my great sword — that sword! — and when he had sung it he died. Messengers carried the news to the capital. His consorts and children came down, made a tomb there, and crawled about the rice fields around it, weeping and singing. Then Yamato Takeru turned into a great white bird eight fathoms long, rose into the sky and flew towards the shore. His consorts and children followed, their bare feet cut on bamboo stubble, feeling no pain, singing as they went. The text says these four songs were all sung at his funeral, and so they are sung at the great funerals of the Heavenly Sovereigns to this day. The white bird stopped at Shiki in Kawachi, and a tomb was made there called the Tomb of the White Bird. But from there it rose into the sky again and flew away.
sections.bodyZh: 到了能烦野，倭建命思念故乡，唱道：大和是国中最好的地方，层层叠叠的青山像垣墙一样环绕，大和啊，多么美好。又唱：愿那些性命完好的人，把平群山上的熊白梼叶插在头上。又唱：啊，从我家那边升起的云啊。病势沉重的时候，他唱了最后一首歌：我把那把大刀留在了少女的床边——那把刀啊！唱完就死了。使者把消息报告给京城。他的妃子和孩子们赶来，在那里修了陵墓，在周围的稻田里爬来爬去，哭着唱歌。这时，倭建命化作一只八寻长的白鸟，飞上天空，向海边飞去。妃子和孩子们在后面追，赤脚被竹子的残茬划破也不觉得痛，一边追一边唱。书中说，这四首歌都在他的葬礼上唱过，所以直到今天，天皇的大葬还唱这些歌。白鸟飞到河内的志几停了下来，人们在那里修了陵墓，叫作白鸟御陵。可是白鸟又从那里飞上天空，飞走了。
sections.evidenceNote: 《古事记》张伯伦译本第八十九至九十节。
sections.headingEn: The songs of home and the white bird

stories.canonicalTitle: Kalevala, Part 1: the making of the world and the Sampo
stories.editorialNote: 依据克劳福德 1888 年英译《卡勒瓦拉》第一至十章，按诗章顺序讲述。《卡勒瓦拉》是隆洛特在十九世纪根据芬兰与卡累利阿的民间口传诗歌编成的史诗，与民间原始唱本并不完全相同；本篇讲述的是隆洛特的编排。克劳福德的人名拼写（如 Wainamoinen、Pohyola）已改为现代通行拼法。

series.labelEn: Part 1: the world and the Sampo
series.labelZh: 第一部 · 创世与三宝

stories.summaryEn: Ilmatar, daughter of the air, descends to the sea and floats for ages; a duck lays eggs on her knee, and the broken eggs become earth, sky, sun, moon and stars. Her son Väinämöinen spends thirty summers in the womb and is born already old. He sows the forests and the barley, and sings the young challenger Joukahainen into a swamp; to save his life Joukahainen promises him his sister Aino, who drowns herself in the sea. Seeking a bride in the northern land of Pohjola, Väinämöinen is shot into the sea by Joukahainen and carried north by an eagle. Louhi, mistress of Pohjola, will send him home if the Sampo is forged for her. On the way he builds a boat for the maiden weaving on the rainbow, gashes his knee with his axe, and is healed by an old man once he has told the origin of iron. At home he tricks the smith Ilmarinen into going north, where Ilmarinen forges the Sampo that grinds grain and wealth — yet the maiden still refuses him.
stories.summaryZh: 大气之女伊尔玛塔尔降到海上，漂流了许多年代，一只鸭子在她的膝盖上下了蛋，蛋碎了，变成了大地、天空、太阳、月亮和星星。她的儿子万奈莫宁在母腹中待了三十个夏天，生下来就是老人。他播种森林与大麦，用歌声把来挑战的年轻歌手约卡海宁唱进沼泽；约卡海宁为了活命，把妹妹艾诺许给了他，艾诺却投海而死。万奈莫宁去北方的波赫约拉求亲，被约卡海宁射落海中，一只鹰把他带到北方。波赫约拉的女主人洛希答应送他回家，条件是为她锻造三宝。回程中他为彩虹上织布的少女造船，被斧头砍伤了膝盖，靠一位老人讲述铁的起源才止住了血。回到家乡，他用计把铁匠伊尔马里宁送到北方，伊尔马里宁锻造出了能磨出粮食与财富的三宝，少女却仍不肯嫁给他。
stories.titleZh: 卡勒瓦拉 · 第一部 创世与三宝

claims.statement: Kalevala Rune I says Ilmatar, daughter of the air, floated on the sea as Water-mother, that a duck laid six golden eggs and one of iron on her raised knee, and that the broken eggs became the earth, the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars and the clouds.

Kalevala Rune I says Ilmatar shaped the headlands, bays and shores, and that Väinämöinen, after thirty summers in her womb, forced his way out, drifted on the sea for years and came ashore already old.

Kalevala Rune II says Väinämöinen had Sampsa Pellervoinen sow the forests, that a little man from the sea grew into a giant and felled the oak that hid the sun and moon, and that Väinämöinen cleared the land for barley, sparing a birch for the birds.

Kalevala Rune III says that when the young Joukahainen challenged Väinämöinen to a contest of wisdom and then to a fight, Väinämöinen sang his sledge, horse and weapons into other shapes and sank him into a swamp up to his chin.

Kalevala Runes III–IV say that Joukahainen, sinking in the swamp, offered bows, boats, horses, gold and fields and at last his sister Aino, whereupon Väinämöinen sang him free; his mother rejoiced, but Aino wept.

Kalevala Rune IV says Aino, refusing to marry the old Väinämöinen, swam out to a rock in the sea that sank with her, and that her mother's tears became three rivers by which three birches and three cuckoos appeared.

Kalevala Rune V says Väinämöinen caught a strange fish that leapt back into the sea and told him it was Aino, whom he had failed to recognise, and that his dead mother then advised him to seek a bride in Pohjola.

Kalevala Rune VI says Joukahainen lay in wait with a steel bow against his mother's warning, and that his third arrow struck Väinämöinen's horse so that Väinämöinen fell into the sea and was swept away.

Kalevala Rune VII says an eagle, remembering the birch he spared, carried Väinämöinen to Pohjola, where Louhi promised to send him home and give her daughter for the forging of a Sampo, which he said only Ilmarinen could make.

Kalevala Rune VIII says the maiden of Pohjola, weaving on the rainbow, set Väinämöinen impossible tasks, and that while building a boat from her spindle his axe, misguided by evil spirits, cut deep into his knee.

Kalevala Rune IX says an old man healed Väinämöinen's knee after Väinämöinen told the origin of iron — born of three maidens' milk, forged by Ilmarinen and made fierce when Hiisi's hornet poisoned the tempering water.

Kalevala Rune X says Väinämöinen tricked Ilmarinen into going to Pohjola, where after rejecting a bow, a boat, a heifer and a plough he forged the Sampo with its many-coloured lid, which Louhi locked in her stone mountain while the maiden refused him.

events.summaryEn: In the oldest times there was a maiden, daughter of the air, named Ilmatar.
events.summaryZh: 在最古老的时候，有一位少女，她是大气的女儿，名叫伊尔玛塔尔。
events.titleEn: The daughter of the air and the duck's eggs

events.summaryEn: With the world given shape, Ilmatar floated on for many years and began to form the land: where she pointed her hand, headlands rose; where she pressed with her foot, deep pools for the fish were made; where she lay on her side, smooth shores appeared; where her feet touched, bays were formed, and where her head rested, harbours.
events.summaryZh: 世界有了形状，伊尔玛塔尔又在海上漂了许多年，开始塑造大地的样子：她把手一指，就出现了岬角；用脚一踩，就有了鱼儿栖息的深坑；侧身一躺，就形成了平滑的海岸；她脚踏过的地方成了海湾，头枕过的地方成了港口。

events.summaryEn: Coming ashore, Väinämöinen saw that the land was bare and nothing grew.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁上了岸，看见大地光秃秃的，什么也不长。
events.titleEn: The sowing and the great oak

events.summaryEn: The fame of Väinämöinen's songs and wisdom spread far and wide.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁的歌声和智慧传遍了四方。

events.summaryEn: Sunk in the swamp, Joukahainen was terrified and began to beg.
events.summaryZh: 约卡海宁陷在沼泽里，吓坏了，开始求饶。

events.summaryEn: Aino went into the woods to break birch twigs for a bath-whisk and met Väinämöinen there.
events.summaryZh: 艾诺到林中去折桦树枝做浴帚，在那里遇见了万奈莫宁。

events.summaryEn: Hearing that Aino was dead, Väinämöinen grieved day and night.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁听说艾诺死了，日夜悲伤。
events.titleEn: The fish and the lost bride

events.summaryEn: Väinämöinen mounted a horse as light as a pea-stalk and set off over the waves for northern Pohjola.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁骑上一匹轻得像豆秆一样的马，踏着海浪向北方的波赫约拉出发。

events.summaryEn: Väinämöinen drifted on the sea for many days, cold and hungry, with no shore in sight.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁在海上漂了许多天，又冷又饿，看不到岸。

events.summaryEn: Driving south in his sledge, Väinämöinen heard the sound of a loom above him.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁赶着雪橇往南走，忽然听见头顶传来织布机的声音。
events.titleEn: The maiden on the rainbow and the axe

events.summaryEn: Bleeding, Väinämöinen drove on in search of a healer.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁流着血，赶着雪橇去找能治伤的人。

events.summaryEn: Back home, Väinämöinen urged the smith Ilmarinen to go north, forge the Sampo and win the maiden of Pohjola.
events.summaryZh: 万奈莫宁回到家，劝铁匠伊尔马里宁到北方去锻造三宝、娶波赫约拉的少女。

versions.labelEn: Kalevala, Runes I–X (Crawford translation, long retelling)
versions.labelZh: 《卡勒瓦拉》第一至十章（克劳福德译本，长篇讲述）
versions.narrativeScope: 大气之女与鸭蛋、万奈莫宁的诞生、播种与大橡树、约卡海宁的挑战、艾诺的命运、鱼与失去的新娘、约卡海宁的箭、鹰与洛希、彩虹上的少女与斧伤、铁的起源、伊尔马里宁被送往北方、锻造三宝
versions.rightsNote: 克劳福德 1888 年英译本属公共领域；本站发布按诗章顺序的独立讲述，人名采用现代芬兰语通行拼法。

sections.bodyEn: In the oldest times there was a maiden, daughter of the air, named Ilmatar. She lived alone for ages in the empty spaces of the sky until she grew weary of it, and came down to the boundless sea. The wind raised the waves, and the waves made her with child; she became the Water-mother and floated on the sea for seven hundred years without giving birth. She cried to Ukko, the highest god, to free her from her pain. Soon a beautiful duck came flying over the waters looking for a place to nest, but there was no land anywhere. Ilmatar raised her knee from the water; the duck took it for a little island, built her nest on it and laid six golden eggs and a seventh of iron. As the duck brooded, Ilmatar felt her knee grow hotter and hotter until it seemed to burn, and she moved it; the eggs rolled into the sea and broke. But the pieces did not perish: the lower halves of the shells became the earth, the upper halves the high vault of heaven, the yolk the sun, the white the moon, the specks on the shells the stars, and the dark fragments the clouds of the sky.
sections.bodyZh: 在最古老的时候，有一位少女，她是大气的女儿，名叫伊尔玛塔尔。她独自在空旷的天空中住了很久很久，渐渐觉得寂寞，就从天上降下来，落到了无边无际的大海上。狂风吹起了海浪，海浪使她怀了孕，她成了“水之母”，在海上漂流了七百年，却始终生不出孩子来。她向至高的天神乌戈哀求，请他来帮助她摆脱痛苦。不久，一只美丽的鸭子在海面上飞来飞去，想找一个地方筑巢，却到处找不到陆地。伊尔玛塔尔从水里抬起膝盖，鸭子以为那是一座小岛，就落在她的膝盖上筑了巢，下了六个金蛋，第七个是铁蛋。鸭子孵着蛋，伊尔玛塔尔觉得膝盖越来越烫，像要被火烧着一样，忍不住动了一下，蛋就滚进海里，摔碎了。可是蛋的碎片并没有消失：下半部的蛋壳变成了大地，上半部变成了高高的天穹，蛋黄变成了太阳，蛋白变成了月亮，蛋壳上的斑点变成了星星，黑色的碎片变成了天上的云。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第一章。
sections.headingEn: The daughter of the air and the duck's eggs

sections.bodyEn: With the world given shape, Ilmatar floated on for many years and began to form the land: where she pointed her hand, headlands rose; where she pressed with her foot, deep pools for the fish were made; where she lay on her side, smooth shores appeared; where her feet touched, bays were formed, and where her head rested, harbours. But her son had not yet been born. Väinämöinen stayed in his mother's womb thirty summers and as many winters, growing in the dark. He prayed to the sun, the moon and the Great Bear: open a way for me out of this narrow place, that I may see the sun and moon in the sky. No answer came. So he pushed open the castle gate with his ring finger, slid back the bony bolt with the toes of his left foot, crawled out of his mother's body and plunged headlong into the sea. He drifted on the waves for years until he came to a nameless headland and climbed ashore. Väinämöinen, later called the eternal singer, was already an old man at his birth.
sections.bodyZh: 世界有了形状，伊尔玛塔尔又在海上漂了许多年，开始塑造大地的样子：她把手一指，就出现了岬角；用脚一踩，就有了鱼儿栖息的深坑；侧身一躺，就形成了平滑的海岸；她脚踏过的地方成了海湾，头枕过的地方成了港口。可是她的儿子还没有出生。万奈莫宁在母亲的腹中待了三十个夏天，又待了同样多的冬天，在黑暗中渐渐长大。他向太阳、月亮和大熊星祈求：请给我打开一条道路，让我走出这狭小的地方，去看看天空的太阳和月亮。可是没有回应。于是他自己用无名指推开了城堡的门，用左脚的脚趾拨开了骨头的门闩，从母亲的身体里爬了出来，一头扎进了海里。他在海浪中漂了好几年，终于来到一片无名的海岬，爬上了岸。这位后来被称为“永恒的歌者”的万奈莫宁，一出生就已经是一个老人了。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第一章。

sections.bodyEn: Coming ashore, Väinämöinen saw that the land was bare and nothing grew. He called the sower Sampsa Pellervoinen to scatter seed over the earth: pines on the hills, firs on the knolls, birches in the swamps, alders in the lowlands, willows in the wet places, bird-cherries by the rivers. Every tree grew except the oak. Then a giant from the sea planted an acorn, and the oak grew so great that its crown hid the clouds and blocked the sun and moon, and the earth was dark. Väinämöinen prayed to his mother to send someone to fell it. A little man rose from the sea, no taller than a thumb, armoured in copper; in a moment he grew into a giant reaching the sky, and with three strokes of his axe he felled the oak, and the sunlight returned. Then Väinämöinen began to sow barley. A titmouse told him to burn the forest first. He felled the whole forest but left one birch for the birds to rest in; an eagle, thankful, struck fire to burn the clearing for him. He sowed the grain, prayed to Ukko for rain, and the barley grew.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁上了岸，看见大地光秃秃的，什么也不长。他请来播种者桑普萨·佩勒沃伊宁，让他在大地上撒下种子：山上种松树，山丘种冷杉，沼泽长桦树，低地长赤杨，湿地长柳树，河岸长稠李。树木都长起来了，只有橡树不肯发芽。后来一位从海里来的巨人帮忙，把一颗橡子种了下去，这棵橡树长得太大了，树冠遮住了天上的云，挡住了太阳和月亮，大地一片黑暗。万奈莫宁祈求母亲派人来砍倒它。海里走上来一个小小的男人，只有拇指那么高，穿着铜甲；可一转眼，他就长成了顶天立地的巨人，挥斧三下，把大橡树砍倒了，阳光重新照到大地上。接着，万奈莫宁开始种大麦。一只山雀告诉他：要先烧林开荒。他砍倒了整片森林，只留下一棵白桦，让鸟儿有地方栖息；一只鹰为此感谢他，替他打火烧林。他撒下麦种，向乌戈祈雨，大麦就长了出来。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第二章。
sections.headingEn: The sowing and the great oak

sections.bodyEn: The fame of Väinämöinen's songs and wisdom spread far and wide. In the north lived a young singer named Joukahainen, who could not bear to hear that anyone sang better than he. Against his parents' warnings he drove off in his sledge to challenge Väinämöinen. Their sledges met head-on on the road and their reins tangled. Joukahainen began to boast of his learning — where the fish spawn, what trees grow on the hills, how heaven and earth were made — and even claimed that he had made the world. Väinämöinen answered that this was the lore of children and women, and that Joukahainen had been present at none of it. Stung, the young man challenged him to fight with swords. Scorning to fight, Väinämöinen began to sing. As he sang, Joukahainen's sledge became bushes by a lake, his horse a stone by the river, his bow a rainbow over the water, his arrows hawks in the sky, and he himself sank little by little into a swamp, the mire rising to his waist, to his breast, to his chin. This is the Kalevala's famous singing contest: the two singers compete not in strength but in knowing the origins of things, and in this epic to know where a thing came from is to have power over it.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁的歌声和智慧传遍了四方。北方有一个年轻的歌手，名叫约卡海宁，听说有人唱得比他好，心里很不服气，不顾父母的劝阻，赶着雪橇去找万奈莫宁比试。两架雪橇在路上迎面相撞，缰绳缠在一起。约卡海宁开始炫耀自己的学问，说起鱼儿在哪里产卵、山上长着什么树、天地是怎样造成的，甚至说世界是他造的。万奈莫宁说：这些都是孩子和女人的学问，你所说的，你都不在场。约卡海宁恼羞成怒，要和他拔剑决斗。万奈莫宁不屑与他相斗，就唱起歌来。随着他的歌声，约卡海宁的雪橇变成了湖边的灌木，马变成了河边的石头，弓变成了水上的彩虹，箭变成了天上的鹰，他自己则一点点沉进了沼泽，泥水没过了腰，没过了胸，一直没到了下巴。这是《卡勒瓦拉》里有名的“唱歌比赛”：两位歌手比的不是力气，而是谁知道万物的起源；而在这部史诗里，知道一样东西的来历，就意味着拥有支配它的力量。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第三章。

sections.bodyEn: Sunk in the swamp, Joukahainen was terrified and began to beg. 'Let me go, and I will give you two fine bows.' Väinämöinen would not take them and sang on. 'I will give you two boats... two swift horses... a helmet full of gold and a hat full of silver... all my fields and harvest.' Väinämöinen refused them all, and the mire rose higher. At last Joukahainen said: 'I will give you my sister Aino, to sweep your house, bake your bread and weave your cloth, and be your wife.' At this Väinämöinen rejoiced; he sat down on a stone of joy and sang his song backwards, and Joukahainen rose out of the swamp, and his horse, sledge and bow returned to their own shapes. Joukahainen went home crestfallen and told his mother he had promised his sister to old Väinämöinen. But his mother was glad: it was what she had always hoped for, to have the great sage as her son-in-law. Only Aino, hearing it, sat down on the steps and wept. So a maiden's marriage was settled in a contest between two men, and no one had asked her a single word.
sections.bodyZh: 约卡海宁陷在沼泽里，吓坏了，开始求饶。他说：放了我吧，我给你两张好弓；万奈莫宁不要，继续往下唱。他又说：我给你两条船；我给你两匹快马；我给你满盔的金子和满帽的银子；我给你所有的田地和庄稼。万奈莫宁都不要，泥水越升越高。最后，约卡海宁说：我把妹妹艾诺许给你，让她给你打扫屋子、烤面包、织布，做你的妻子。万奈莫宁听了，心里非常欢喜，就坐在一块喜悦的石头上，把刚才的歌倒过来唱了一遍，约卡海宁从沼泽里升了上来，马、雪橇和弓箭也都恢复了原样。约卡海宁垂头丧气地回到家，告诉母亲他把妹妹许给了老万奈莫宁。母亲却高兴地说：这正是我一直盼望的事，能有那位大智者做女婿。只有艾诺听了，坐在台阶上哭了起来。一个少女的婚事，就这样在两个男人的较量中被定了下来，而她本人一句话也没有被问过。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第三至四章。

sections.bodyEn: Aino went into the woods to break birch twigs for a bath-whisk and met Väinämöinen there. 'Maiden,' said the old man, 'wear your beads and cross for no one but me.' Aino tore the cross from her breast, the rings from her fingers, the beads from her neck and the ribbons from her hair, threw them on the ground, and ran home weeping. Her mother told her not to weep, but to open the chest in the loft and put on her finest clothes and her gold and silver — things her mother had woven and kept for her wedding when she was young. Aino said she would rather be the bride of the salmon in the sea than the staff of an old man. She put on her finest clothes, left home, walked for days, and came to the sea. Seeing three maidens bathing, she took off her clothes and swam out to a bright-coloured rock. The rock sank to the bottom, and Aino sank with it and never came back. A hare carried the news home. Her mother wept so long that her tears became three rivers; three birches grew by them, and on the birches sat three cuckoos, one calling love, one calling bridegroom, one calling joy. The mother later says in her grief: mothers, never force a daughter to marry a man she does not want.
sections.bodyZh: 艾诺到林中去折桦树枝做浴帚，在那里遇见了万奈莫宁。老人说：少女啊，不要为别人戴珠子和十字架，只为我戴吧。艾诺扯下胸前的十字架、手上的戒指、颈上的珠子和头上的发带，扔在地上，哭着跑回家去。母亲劝她不要哭，叫她打开阁楼上的箱子，穿上最好的衣服，戴上金银首饰——那都是母亲年轻时织的、留给她出嫁用的。艾诺却说：我宁愿嫁给大海里的鲑鱼，也不愿做老人的拐杖。她穿上最好的衣服，离开家，一连走了好几天，来到海边。她看见三个少女在海里洗澡，就脱下衣服，游到海中的一块彩色岩石上。岩石却沉进了海底，艾诺也跟着沉了下去，再也没有回来。一只野兔把消息带回了她的家。母亲哭了很久，她的眼泪流成了三条河，河边长出了三棵白桦，桦树上落下三只杜鹃，一只唱着“爱啊”，一只唱着“新郎啊”，一只唱着“欢乐啊”。诗中母亲后来悔恨地说：做母亲的人啊，千万不要逼女儿嫁给她不喜欢的人。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第四章。

sections.bodyEn: Hearing that Aino was dead, Väinämöinen grieved day and night. He went to the sea to fish and after long fishing caught a strange fish — not a salmon, not a trout, not like any fish he had seen. He took out his knife to cut it up for breakfast, but the fish leapt from his hand back into the sea, raised its head from the water near the boat, and said: 'I am no salmon for your breakfast. I am Aino, Joukahainen's sister, the maiden you sought. I would have been your wife, made your bed and cooked your food, but you did not know me.' Then it sank into the depths. Väinämöinen cast his nets and lines again and again but never found that fish. He went home in sorrow, feeling old and joyless. Then his dead mother woke in her grave beneath the waves and said: 'Do not grieve for Joukahainen's sister. Go north to Pohjola, where there are maidens fairer and wiser.'
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁听说艾诺死了，日夜悲伤。他到海边去钓鱼，钓了很久，钓上来一条奇怪的鱼，它不像鲑鱼，不像鳟鱼，也不像任何他见过的鱼。他拿出刀来，想把它剖开做早饭，那条鱼却从他手里一跃而起，跳回了海里，在离船不远的水面上抬起头来说：我不是给你做早饭的鲑鱼。我就是艾诺，约卡海宁的妹妹，你想娶的那个少女。我本想做你的妻子，为你铺床、做饭，可你没有认出我来。说完，它就沉入了深海。万奈莫宁拼命撒网、垂钓，再也找不到那条鱼了。他悲伤地回到家里，觉得自己老了，再也没有欢乐了。这时，他已故的母亲从海浪下的坟墓里醒来，对他说：不要为约卡海宁的妹妹悲伤，到北方的波赫约拉去吧，那里有更美丽、更聪明的少女。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第五章。
sections.headingEn: The fish and the lost bride

sections.bodyEn: Väinämöinen mounted a horse as light as a pea-stalk and set off over the waves for northern Pohjola. But Joukahainen had never forgotten his shame in the swamp. He made a bow of steel, strung it with a string like a serpent's sinew, shaped his arrows and dipped them in poison, and lay in wait by the way. His mother begged him not to shoot: Väinämöinen was the singer of the land, and if he died, joy and song would vanish from the world. He would not listen. His first arrow flew too high, into the clouds; his second too low, into the earth; his third struck the horse beneath Väinämöinen. The horse fell, Väinämöinen tumbled into the sea, and the wind and waves carried him away. Joukahainen went home and boasted to his mother that he had killed old Väinämöinen. 'You have done an evil thing,' she said. 'You have shot the best singer on earth.' Joukahainen's mother was right: in the Kalevala song is power and the source of the world's joy. But the eternal singer did not die; the sea bore him up, as it had at his birth, and carried him far away. Drifting helpless on the waves, he was far from home and drawing ever nearer to the north.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁骑上一匹轻得像豆秆一样的马，踏着海浪向北方的波赫约拉出发。约卡海宁却一直记恨着沼泽里的耻辱。他做了一张钢弓，配上蛇筋一样的弓弦，削好了箭，蘸上了毒，埋伏在路边等着。母亲劝他不要射，说万奈莫宁是大地的歌者，他死了，世上的欢乐和歌声都会消失。约卡海宁不听。他射出第一支箭，飞得太高，射进了云里；第二支箭飞得太低，钻进了地下；第三支箭射中了万奈莫宁胯下的马。马倒下了，万奈莫宁跌进了大海，被风浪卷走了。约卡海宁回家得意地告诉母亲：我射死了老万奈莫宁。母亲说：你做了一件坏事，你射死了大地上最好的歌者。约卡海宁的母亲说得没错：在《卡勒瓦拉》里，歌声就是力量，也是世间欢乐的来源。好在这位“永恒的歌者”并没有死，大海托着他，像当年他出生时一样，把他带向远方。万奈莫宁在海浪中漂流，无依无靠，这时他已经离家很远，离北方的波赫约拉却越来越近了。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第六章。

sections.bodyEn: Väinämöinen drifted on the sea for many days, cold and hungry, with no shore in sight. Then a great eagle came flying from the edge of the sky. Remembering that when Väinämöinen burned the forest he had left a birch for the birds, it said: 'You left the birds a tree to rest in; now I will repay you.' It took him on its back and carried him to the shore of northern Pohjola, set him down and flew away. Väinämöinen wept on the strange shore, and his weeping reached Louhi, the mistress of Pohjola. The gap-toothed Louhi came in her boat, found him, took him home, fed him and restored his strength. He said he longed to go home. Louhi said: 'I will send you home and give you my daughter too, if you will forge me a Sampo from the tip of a swan's feather, the milk of a barren cow, a grain of barley and the wool of a summer ewe.' Väinämöinen answered: 'I cannot forge the Sampo, but in my land there is a smith, Ilmarinen, who forged the vault of the sky; he can.' Louhi agreed, gave him a sledge, and warned him not to look up at the sky on his way home. Pohjola, the north, is in the epic a cold and mighty land, and its mistress Louhi, skilled in magic and cunning, becomes the hardest adversary of the heroes of Kalevala.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁在海上漂了许多天，又冷又饿，看不到岸。这时，一只巨大的鹰从天边飞来，它记得当年万奈莫宁烧林时为鸟儿留下了一棵白桦，就对他说：你曾经为鸟儿留下了栖息的树，现在我来报答你。它让万奈莫宁骑在背上，一直把他驮到北方的波赫约拉海边，放下他就飞走了。万奈莫宁在陌生的海岸上哭泣，哭声传到了波赫约拉的女主人洛希那里。缺了牙的洛希坐船来找到他，把他带回家里，给他吃喝，让他恢复了力气。万奈莫宁说他想回家。洛希说：我可以送你回去，还把女儿嫁给你，只要你为我锻造一件三宝：用天鹅的羽毛尖、不生育的母牛的奶、一粒大麦和夏天母羊的一缕羊毛把它造出来。万奈莫宁说：我不会锻造三宝，可是我家乡有一位铁匠伊尔马里宁，他锻造过天空的穹顶，他一定能做到。洛希答应了，给了他一架雪橇，叮嘱他回家的路上千万不要抬头看天。北方的波赫约拉在史诗里是一片寒冷而强大的土地，它的女主人洛希会魔法、有心计，后来成了卡勒瓦拉英雄们最难对付的对手。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第七章。

sections.bodyEn: Driving south in his sledge, Väinämöinen heard the sound of a loom above him. Forgetting Louhi's warning he looked up, and there sat the beautiful maiden of Pohjola on the rainbow, weaving with a golden shuttle and silver thread. He asked her to come down into his sledge and go home with him. She said he must first do certain things: split a horsehair with a knife that had no edge, and tie an egg into knots no one could see; peel the bark from a stone, and cut stakes from the ice without splintering it. He did them all. Then she said: 'Build a boat from the fragments of my spindle and launch it without pushing it with hand or knee.' Väinämöinen set to building on a blue stone, but the evil spirits Hiisi and Lempo made his axe slip, and it cut into his knee. Blood gushed out like a river, flooding the meadows and the hills. He knew many charms, but not the one to stop a wound of iron, for he did not know the origin of iron.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁赶着雪橇往南走，忽然听见头顶传来织布机的声音。他忘了洛希的叮嘱，抬头一看，波赫约拉的美丽少女正坐在彩虹上，用金梭银线织着布。万奈莫宁请她坐到自己的雪橇上来，跟他回家。少女说，要她跟他走，他得先做几件事：用一把没有刃的刀劈开一根马鬃，把一个鸡蛋打成看不出的结；剥下石头的皮，从冰上砍下木桩而不溅起一点碎屑。万奈莫宁一件件都做到了。少女又说：你还要用我纺锤的碎片造一艘船，不用手推、不用膝顶，把它推下水去。万奈莫宁在一块蓝色的石头上造船，可是恶灵希西和勒姆波暗中作怪，让他的斧头一滑，砍进了自己的膝盖。鲜血像河水一样涌出来，淹没了草地和山丘。万奈莫宁会许多咒语，却唯独想不起止住铁伤的那一首，因为他不知道铁的起源。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第八章。
sections.headingEn: The maiden on the rainbow and the axe

sections.bodyEn: Bleeding, Väinämöinen drove on in search of a healer. He passed house after house until, in a small hut, he found a white-bearded old man, who said: 'I have stopped greater floods of blood than this. But first tell me the origin of iron.' So Väinämöinen told it: in the beginning three maidens sprinkled their milk from the sky over the earth; the black milk became soft iron, the white became steel, the red became hard iron. Iron, afraid of fire, hid in the swamps and springs, under the footprints of the wolf and the bear. The smith Ilmarinen found it and put it into his furnace, and the iron begged him not to harm it, promising never to wound its kin. But as Ilmarinen tempered the steel, Hiisi's bird, a hornet, came and slipped the venom of serpents, the acid of ants and the poison of toads into the tempering water, so the steel became fierce, broke its oath and would cut even its own brothers. When the old man had heard it, he loudly rebuked iron for its wickedness, spoke the charms that stop blood, and sent his son to boil a salve, and bound the wound. It healed; Väinämöinen thanked Ukko and drove home.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁流着血，赶着雪橇去找能治伤的人。他走过一户户人家，最后在一座小屋里找到了一位白胡子老人。老人说：比这更大的伤我也治过。可你得先告诉我铁是怎么来的。万奈莫宁就讲起了铁的起源：最早的时候，三位少女在天上把乳汁洒向大地，黑色的乳汁变成了软铁，白色的乳汁变成了钢，红色的乳汁变成了生铁。铁害怕火，躲进了沼泽和泉水里，藏在狼和熊的脚印下面。铁匠伊尔马里宁找到了它，把它放进熔炉里锻炼，铁哀求他不要伤害它，答应永远不伤害自己的亲人。可伊尔马里宁在给钢淬火时，希西的鸟——一只胡蜂——飞来，把毒蛇的毒液、蚂蚁的酸液和蛤蟆的毒汁偷偷放进了淬火的水里，钢从此变得凶猛，背叛了誓言，连自己的兄弟都要砍伤。老人听完，大声斥责铁的罪恶，念起了止血的咒语，又派儿子去熬制药膏，替万奈莫宁包扎了伤口。伤口愈合了，万奈莫宁感谢乌戈，赶着雪橇回到了家乡。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第九章。

sections.bodyEn: Back home, Väinämöinen urged the smith Ilmarinen to go north, forge the Sampo and win the maiden of Pohjola. Ilmarinen refused to go to that cold land that eats men. So Väinämöinen sang up a flowering fir with the moon in its crown and the Great Bear in its branches, and coaxed Ilmarinen to climb up and fetch the moon; when he reached the top, Väinämöinen sang up a whirlwind that swept Ilmarinen away and carried him to Pohjola. Louhi welcomed him and asked whether he could forge the Sampo. Ilmarinen built a furnace on a rock, set thralls to work the bellows, and put the swan's feather tip, the milk, the barley and the wool into the fire. On the first day a golden bow came out, but it wanted a head every day, so he broke it; on the second a red boat that wanted only war; on the third a heifer with golden horns, too ill-tempered; on the fourth a golden plough that ploughed other men's fields — all thrown back into the fire. He called the four winds, which blew for three days and nights, and at last the Sampo took shape, with a many-coloured lid; on one side it ground grain for eating, on another for selling, on a third for storing, a great measure each day. Louhi rejoiced and locked the Sampo in the stone mountain of Pohjola behind nine locks, its roots sunk nine fathoms deep. But the maiden said she would not yet leave her mother's house, and Ilmarinen went home crestfallen in the boat Louhi gave him.
sections.bodyZh: 万奈莫宁回到家，劝铁匠伊尔马里宁到北方去锻造三宝、娶波赫约拉的少女。伊尔马里宁说：我不去那个吃人的阴冷地方。万奈莫宁就唱出一棵开着花的冷杉，树梢上挂着月亮，枝间停着大熊星，骗伊尔马里宁爬上去摘月亮；等他爬到树顶，万奈莫宁唱起一阵狂风，把伊尔马里宁连人带树卷走，一直吹到了波赫约拉。洛希热情地款待他，问他能不能锻造三宝。伊尔马里宁找到一块石头砌起熔炉，叫奴隶们拉风箱，把天鹅的羽毛尖、母牛的奶、大麦和羊毛放进火里。第一天，炉中出来一张金弓，可它每天都要一颗人头，他把它折断了；第二天出来一艘红船，它专要去打仗；第三天出来一头金角母牛，脾气太坏；第四天出来一把金犁，专犁别人的田地，都被他扔回了火里。他唤来四方的风，风吹了三天三夜，三宝终于成形了，它有一个五彩的盖子，一边磨出吃的粮食，一边磨出卖的粮食，一边磨出存的粮食，每天各磨一大斗。洛希非常高兴，把三宝锁进波赫约拉的石山里，上了九道锁，三宝的根扎进地下九寻深。可是少女说她还不想离开母亲的家，伊尔马里宁只好垂头丧气地坐上洛希给的船，回到了家乡。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十章。

stories.canonicalTitle: Kalevala, Part 2: Lemminkäinen
stories.editorialNote: 依据克劳福德 1888 年英译《卡勒瓦拉》第十一至十五章，按诗章顺序讲述。隆洛特在编排勒明凯宁的故事时合并了民间不同英雄的唱本，本篇讲述的是隆洛特的编排；勒明凯宁被砍碎的情节照原诗交代结果，不渲染细节。
stories.summaryEn: The handsome, reckless Lemminkäinen carries off the maiden Kyllikki from the island of Saari, and they vow — he never to go to war, she never to go dancing in the village. When she breaks her vow, he sets out for northern Pohjola to woo another. His mother begs him to stay; he flings his brush at the wall: when it bleeds, misfortune has befallen me. In Pohjola he sings all the sorcerers away but spares an old blind herdsman, whom he mocks. Louhi sets him three tasks: to catch the elk of Hiisi on skis, to bridle Hiisi's fire-breathing horse, and to shoot the swan on the black river of Tuonela. He does the first two; at the third, the blind herdsman pierces his heart with a water-serpent and throws him into the river, where the son of the lord of the dead hews him to pieces. At home the brush drips blood. His mother hurries north, learns the truth from Louhi and the sun, has the smith forge a long-handled copper rake, gathers her son's body piece by piece from the river, joins his veins, and sends a bee beyond the nine heavens for the Creator's honey, until her son lives again.
stories.summaryZh: 英俊而鲁莽的勒明凯宁从萨里岛抢走了少女基利基，两人立誓：他不再去打仗，她不再去村里跳舞。基利基破了誓，勒明凯宁就要到北方的波赫约拉去另求新娘。母亲苦苦相劝，他把梳子往墙上一掷，说：梳子流血的时候，就是我遭难的时候。他在波赫约拉用歌声赶走了所有的巫师，只放过了一个又老又瞎、被他嘲笑的牧人。洛希给他出了三道难题：滑雪追捕希西的麋鹿，给希西喷火的马套上笼头，射死图奥内拉黑河上的天鹅。前两件他都做到了，第三件时，那个盲眼牧人在河边用一条水蛇刺穿了他的心，把他抛进黑河，亡者之王的儿子把他砍成了碎块。家中的梳子流出了血。母亲赶到北方，从洛希和太阳那里问出真相，请铁匠打了一把长柄铜耙，从黑河里一块块捞出儿子的身体，缝合血脉，又派蜜蜂从九重天外取来神的蜜膏，终于让儿子活了过来。
stories.titleZh: 卡勒瓦拉 · 第二部 勒明凯宁

claims.statement: Kalevala Rune XI says the reckless Lemminkäinen went to the island of Saari to woo Kyllikki, who had refused the sons of the sun, moon and stars, and befriended all the island maidens except her.
Kalevala Rune XI says Lemminkäinen carried Kyllikki off in his sledge, and that they swore before Ukko that he would never go to war and she would never go dancing in the village.

Kalevala Rune XII says Kyllikki broke her vow and went dancing in the village while Lemminkäinen was fishing, and that when his sister Ainikki told him he declared himself free of his own oath and set out for Pohjola.
Kalevala Rune XII says that, ignoring his mother's warnings, Lemminkäinen threw down his brush saying that when it dripped blood misfortune would have befallen him, and drove north to Pohjola.
Kalevala Rune XII says Lemminkäinen sang all the sorcerers of Pohjola away except the old blind herdsman Märkähattu, whom he mocked, and who went in hatred to wait by the river of Tuonela.
Kalevala Rune XIII says Louhi set Lemminkäinen the task of catching the elk of Hiisi on skis, and that he chased the elk Hiisi had made into Lapland until his ski and pole broke and the elk escaped.
Kalevala Rune XIV says that after praying for three days to the forest gods Tapio and Mielikki, Lemminkäinen caught the elk of Hiisi and brought it to Louhi, who then set him a second task.
Kalevala Rune XIV says that when Louhi set him to bridle Hiisi's fire-breathing gelding, Lemminkäinen prayed Ukko to quench it with hail and then bridled it with a golden halter.

Kalevala Rune XIV says that when Lemminkäinen went to shoot the swan of Tuonela, the blind herdsman Märkähattu, lying in wait, pierced his heart with a water-serpent, and he lamented that he had never learned the charm against it.
Kalevala Rune XIV says the herdsman threw the dying Lemminkäinen into the black river of Tuonela, where the son of Tuoni hewed him into pieces and cast them into its depths.

Kalevala Rune XV says that when the brush dripped blood Lemminkäinen's mother hurried to Pohjola, forced Louhi to tell where she had sent him, and after the trees, the road and the moon could not help, learned from the sun that he lay hewn in pieces in the river of Tuonela.

Kalevala Rune XV says Lemminkäinen's mother raked her son's body piece by piece from the river of Tuonela with a copper rake forged by Ilmarinen, had his veins joined, and revived him with the Creator's honey brought by a bee from beyond the nine heavens.

events.summaryEn: Lemminkäinen, also called Ahti and Kaukomieli, was a handsome young man with ruddy cheeks and fine hair, but wild and reckless, his eyes always roving after the maidens.
events.summaryZh: 勒明凯宁又叫阿赫蒂、考科米耶利，是一个英俊的年轻人，脸颊红润，头发漂亮，可是性情放荡不羁，眼睛总是在少女们身上打转。

events.summaryEn: One evening the maidens were dancing in a forest glade with Kyllikki leading them.
events.summaryZh: 有一天傍晚，少女们在林间空地上跳舞，基利基跳在最前面。

events.summaryEn: The days went by, and Lemminkäinen often went out fishing.
events.summaryZh: 日子一天天过去，勒明凯宁常常出门去打鱼。

events.summaryEn: His mother begged him: 'Do not go to Pohjola.
events.summaryZh: 母亲苦苦劝他：不要去波赫约拉，那里的拉普兰巫师会用歌声把你唱进火里、唱进冰里，你一个人去会丢掉性命的。

events.summaryEn: Arriving in Pohjola, Lemminkäinen went into Louhi's hall, which was full of sorcerers and singers playing and singing; they ignored the stranger.
events.summaryZh: 勒明凯宁来到波赫约拉，走进洛希的大厅，那里坐满了巫师和歌者，弹琴的弹琴，唱歌的唱歌。
events.titleEn: The sorcerers and the blind herdsman

events.summaryEn: Lemminkäinen asked Louhi for her daughter.
events.summaryZh: 勒明凯宁向洛希求娶她的女儿。

events.summaryEn: Lemminkäinen mended his skis, and this time, instead of boasting, he prayed to the forest gods.
events.summaryZh: 勒明凯宁修好了滑雪板，这一次他不再夸口，而是向森林之神祈祷。

events.summaryEn: Louhi said: 'Go and bridle the brown gelding of Hiisi, which runs on Hiisi's meadows breathing fire from its nostrils and smoke from its mouth.' Lemminkäinen set out with a golden halter and a silver bridle.
events.summaryZh: 洛希说：你去把希西那匹棕色的骟马套上笼头，它在希西的原野上奔跑，鼻孔里喷着火，嘴里冒着烟。

events.summaryEn: Louhi said: 'Go to the black river of Tuonela, and with a single arrow shoot the swan there; then my daughter shall be yours.' Tuonela was the land of the dead, and the black river lay in the realm of Tuoni, lord of the dead.
events.summaryZh: 洛希说：你去图奥内拉的黑河上，只射一箭，射死那里的天鹅，我就把女儿给你。

events.summaryEn: The blind herdsman threw the dying Lemminkäinen into the black river of Tuonela, and the current swept him towards the roaring falls.
events.summaryZh: 盲眼牧人把奄奄一息的勒明凯宁扔进了图奥内拉的黑河里，河水把他卷向汹涌的瀑布。
events.titleEn: The pieces in the black river

events.summaryEn: At home, Lemminkäinen's mother watched the brush every day.
events.summaryZh: 在勒明凯宁的家里，母亲每天都看着那把梳子。

events.summaryEn: Weeping, the mother went to the smith Ilmarinen and asked for a rake with copper teeth a hundred fathoms long and a handle five hundred fathoms long, and Ilmarinen forged it.
events.summaryZh: 母亲哭着去找铁匠伊尔马里宁，请他打一把耙子：铜的耙齿要一百寻长，耙柄要五百寻长。
events.titleEn: The copper rake and the bee

versions.narrativeScope: 萨里岛的花、雪橇上的新娘与誓约、破誓、流血的梳子、波赫约拉的巫师与盲牧人、希西的麋鹿、森林之神、火焰之马、图奥内拉的天鹅、黑河里的碎片、母亲的寻找、铜耙与蜜蜂
versions.rightsNote: 克劳福德 1888 年英译本属公共领域；本站发布按诗章顺序的独立讲述，人名采用现代芬兰语通行拼法。

sections.bodyEn: Lemminkäinen, also called Ahti and Kaukomieli, was a handsome young man with ruddy cheeks and fine hair, but wild and reckless, his eyes always roving after the maidens. He heard that on the island of Saari lived a beautiful maiden named Kyllikki, called the flower of Saari, who had refused many suitors — the son of the sun, the son of the moon, the son of the stars, even princes from distant lands. Against his mother's warnings he drove his sledge to Saari. The island maidens mocked him as a poor fellow who could not even feed his horse. He did not take offence; he stayed on the island, played with the maidens by day and danced with them by night, and soon was friends with every maiden there — except Kyllikki, who would not even look at him. But Lemminkäinen had made up his mind: he would have the flower of Saari. His other name, Kaukomieli, means far-minded, and it fits him: he could never stay quietly at home. His mother had warned him that the people of Saari would look down on a poor stranger, but he had to try.
sections.bodyZh: 勒明凯宁又叫阿赫蒂、考科米耶利，是一个英俊的年轻人，脸颊红润，头发漂亮，可是性情放荡不羁，眼睛总是在少女们身上打转。他听说萨里岛上有一位美丽的少女，名叫基利基，被称为“萨里岛之花”，许多求婚者——太阳的儿子、月亮的儿子、星星的儿子，甚至遥远国度的王子——都被她拒绝了。勒明凯宁不顾母亲的劝阻，赶着雪橇来到萨里岛。岛上的少女们嘲笑他，说他是个穷小子，连马都喂不饱。勒明凯宁并不生气，他留在岛上，白天和少女们一起玩耍，晚上和她们一起跳舞，很快就和岛上所有的少女都成了朋友，只有基利基一个人对他不理不睬，从不正眼看他。可是勒明凯宁已经下定了决心：非娶到这朵萨里岛之花不可。他的另一个名字考科米耶利，意思是“心在远方的人”，正好说明了他的性情：他永远不肯安安稳稳地待在家里。母亲曾警告他，萨里岛的人会看不起一个外乡来的穷小子，可他偏偏要去试一试。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十一章。

sections.bodyEn: One evening the maidens were dancing in a forest glade with Kyllikki leading them. Lemminkäinen drove up in his sledge, seized Kyllikki, threw her into the sledge, cracked his whip and sped away. Kyllikki wept and cried out, begging to be let go home: 'Let me go, or I will call my brothers; they will overtake you and cut off your head.' He answered: 'My heart is brave and my sword is sharp; I do not fear your brothers.' She wept that he was a poor man who only knew how to fight. So he promised her: 'I swear never again to go to war, not even for mountains of gold and silver. And you must swear never again to go dancing in the village, however much you long to.' Kyllikki agreed. They swore their oaths before Ukko and went to Lemminkäinen's home, where his mother joyfully welcomed her beautiful daughter-in-law. The two vows bound together two people of opposite nature, a quarrelsome hero and a maiden who loved merrymaking; with the vows, the danger too was laid down.
sections.bodyZh: 有一天傍晚，少女们在林间空地上跳舞，基利基跳在最前面。勒明凯宁赶着雪橇冲过来，一把抱起基利基，把她扔进雪橇，用鞭子一甩，飞驰而去。基利基又哭又喊，求他放她回家，说：放我回去吧，不然我就喊我的兄弟们来，他们会追上你，把你的头砍下来。勒明凯宁说：我的心是勇敢的，我的剑是锋利的，我不怕你的兄弟。基利基哭着说，他是一个只会打仗的穷汉。勒明凯宁就向她许诺：我发誓，从今以后再也不去打仗，哪怕金银堆成山也不去。你也要发誓，从今以后不再到村子里去跳舞，不管多么想去。基利基答应了。两人在乌戈面前立下誓约，回到勒明凯宁的家。母亲欢喜地迎接了这位美丽的儿媳。这两个誓言把两个性情相反的人拴在一起：一个是好斗的英雄，一个是爱热闹的少女。誓言立下了，危险却也一起埋下了。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十一章。

sections.bodyEn: The days went by, and Lemminkäinen often went out fishing. One day he stayed out late on the water, and Kyllikki, weary of being alone at home, broke her vow and slipped off to the village to dance. Lemminkäinen's sister Ainikki saw her and told her brother as soon as he came home. Angry and hurt, he said: 'Kyllikki has broken her oath, so I need not keep mine. I will go to war; I will go north to Pohjola and woo a maiden there.' Kyllikki wept and begged forgiveness, but his mind was made up. He said to his mother: 'Bring my war-coat, bring my sword. I am going to Pohjola, where there are beautiful maidens and many sorcerers waiting for me to match my strength against them.' So the breaking of one vow set the hero back on the road of danger. Ainikki's words to her brother were simple: Kyllikki has gone to a strange village and danced there. That one sentence was enough for Lemminkäinen to think himself released from his own oath. His mother said that the vow had been made by two and half of it still stood, but he would not hear her.
sections.bodyZh: 日子一天天过去，勒明凯宁常常出门去打鱼。有一天他出海很晚还没有回来，基利基一个人在家闷得慌，就违背誓言，偷偷跑到村子里去跳舞了。勒明凯宁的妹妹艾尼基看见了，等哥哥一回来，就把这件事告诉了他。勒明凯宁又气又恼，说：基利基破了她的誓言，那我也不必再守我的誓言了。我要去打仗，我要到北方的波赫约拉去，向那里的少女求婚。基利基哭着请求原谅，他却已经铁了心。他对母亲说：快把我的战衣拿来，把我的剑拿来，我要到波赫约拉去，那里有美丽的少女，还有许多巫师等着我去较量。一个誓言的破灭，就这样把这位英雄重新推上了危险的道路。艾尼基告诉哥哥的话很简单：基利基到别人的村子里去了，在那里和人一起跳舞。这一句话，就让勒明凯宁觉得自己也被誓言解脱了。母亲劝他说，誓言是两个人一起立的，破了一半也还剩一半，可他已经听不进去了。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十二章。

sections.bodyEn: His mother begged him: 'Do not go to Pohjola. The Lapland sorcerers will sing you into fire and ice; alone you will lose your life.' He answered: 'The Lapland sorcerers have sung against me before; I do not fear them.' 'You have a beautiful wife at home,' she said. 'Why seek a bride elsewhere?' He would not listen. He combed his hair and flung the brush against the wall — or by the stove, in some tellings — and said: 'When this brush drips blood, misfortune has befallen me.' His mother and wife wept as he put on his iron mail, girded his sword, harnessed his horse and drove off north. All the way he chanted charms, praying Ukko and the spirits of the forest to guard him and give strength to his sword and horse. The brush left at home became the sign his mother watched day and night. In the whole epic Lemminkäinen's mother is one of the most steadfast and courageous figures. From the moment her son left she began to watch; the story will show that her love runs deeper than the river of the dead. Lemminkäinen never looked back; his mind was already in the north.
sections.bodyZh: 母亲苦苦劝他：不要去波赫约拉，那里的拉普兰巫师会用歌声把你唱进火里、唱进冰里，你一个人去会丢掉性命的。勒明凯宁说：拉普兰的巫师们早就对我唱过歌了，我一点也不怕。母亲说：你有一个美丽的妻子在家，还要去别处找什么新娘？他不听，梳好了头，把梳子往墙上——一说是往炉边——一扔，说：当这把梳子流出血来的时候，就是我遭到不幸的时候。母亲和妻子哭着看他穿上铁甲，佩上宝剑，套好了马，赶着雪橇向北方出发了。他一路上念着咒语，祈求乌戈和森林的神灵保佑他，给他的剑和马增添力量。那把留在家中的梳子，从此成了母亲日夜守望的信号。在整部史诗里，勒明凯宁的母亲是最坚定、最勇敢的人物之一。儿子离开的那一刻，她就开始守望；后面的故事会证明，她的爱比亡者之河还要深。勒明凯宁却头也不回，他的心思已经全在北方。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十二章。

sections.bodyEn: Arriving in Pohjola, Lemminkäinen went into Louhi's hall, which was full of sorcerers and singers playing and singing; they ignored the stranger. He stood in the doorway and began to sing, and song poured from his mouth like fire. He sang the sorcerers away one by one: some into the wilderness, some into the lakes, some into the rapids, some to icebound distant places. At last only one was left in the hall, an old, blind herdsman in a wet hat, named Märkähattu. Lemminkäinen did not sing against him but mocked him: 'You wretched old man, I would not stoop to sing against you; you are blind and ugly, you have wronged your own kin and cannot even tend the cattle.' Shamed and full of hatred, the old herdsman slipped out of the hall, went to the black river of Tuonela, and waited there for the day Lemminkäinen would pass that way. The name Märkähattu means Wet-hat. Lemminkäinen sang away all his mighty rivals but slighted the humblest old man of all, and that slight would cost him his life.
sections.bodyZh: 勒明凯宁来到波赫约拉，走进洛希的大厅，那里坐满了巫师和歌者，弹琴的弹琴，唱歌的唱歌。他们看见这个陌生人，都不理睬他。勒明凯宁就站在门口唱起歌来，歌声像火一样从他口中喷出，他把那些巫师一个个唱走了：有的唱进了荒野，有的唱进了湖里，有的唱进了激流，有的唱到了冰封的远方。最后，大厅里只剩下一个又老又瞎、戴着湿帽子的牧人，叫马尔卡哈图。勒明凯宁没有对他唱歌，反而嘲笑他说：你这个可怜的老头，我才不屑对你唱，你又瞎又丑，连自己的姐妹都敢欺负，连牛都看不好。老牧人受了这番羞辱，心里怀恨，悄悄走出大厅，来到图奥内拉的黑河边，等着勒明凯宁总有一天会从这里经过。马尔卡哈图这个名字，意思是“湿帽子”。勒明凯宁唱走了所有强大的对手，却偏偏轻视了这个最不起眼的老人，这一次轻视，后来要了他的命。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十二章。
sections.headingEn: The sorcerers and the blind herdsman

sections.bodyEn: Lemminkäinen asked Louhi for her daughter. Louhi said: 'You have a wife already, but if you can catch the elk of Hiisi on skis, my daughter shall be yours.' He went to a skilled maker of skis and had a fine pair made, boasting as they were made that no beast in the forest could escape his skis. The evil spirit Hiisi heard, and made an elk out of rotten wood, willow twigs, roots and things of the swamp, and set it running towards Lapland. Lemminkäinen sped after it on his skis, which hissed over the snow as swift as fire. The elk ran wild, burst into the Lapps' huts and kicked over their kettles so that the meat fell into the ashes, and the Lapp women and children wept and laughed. Lemminkäinen thrust down so hard that his ski snapped, and his ski-pole too, and the elk vanished. He stood in the snow, bitterly vexed. The ski-maker is called in the poem Kauppi, also Lyylikki. Hiisi is an evil spirit of the epic, often paired with another, Lempo, in making trouble for the heroes.
sections.bodyZh: 勒明凯宁向洛希求娶她的女儿。洛希说：你已经有妻子了，可要是你能滑雪捉住希西的麋鹿，我就把女儿给你。勒明凯宁找到一个造雪橇板的巧匠，请他做了一副好滑雪板，一边做一边夸口：森林里没有一只野兽能逃过我的滑雪板。恶灵希西听见了，就用朽木、柳枝、草根和沼泽里的东西造出一头麋鹿，让它奔向拉普兰。勒明凯宁滑着雪追了上去，滑雪板在雪地上嘶嘶作响，像火一样飞快。那头麋鹿一路狂奔，冲进拉普兰人的家里，踢翻了锅子，弄得煮好的肉都掉进了灰里，拉普兰的妇女和孩子又哭又笑。勒明凯宁用力过猛，一脚踩下去，滑雪板啪的一声折断了，滑雪杖也断了，麋鹿逃得无影无踪。他站在雪地里，心里懊恼极了。为他做滑雪板的巧匠，原诗里叫考皮，又叫吕利基。希西是史诗里的恶灵，常常和另一个恶灵勒姆波一起，给英雄们制造麻烦。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十三章。

sections.bodyEn: Lemminkäinen mended his skis, and this time, instead of boasting, he prayed to the forest gods. He sang to Tapio, king of the forest, and Mielikki, its mistress: 'Master of the forest, fair mother of the woods, open your treasure-house and drive that elk into my path, and I will repay you with gold and silver.' He sang of the beauty of the forest, of its mother in golden garments, of the trees standing like people in festive dress. For three days he prayed, and the forest gods, moved by his song, drove the elk to him. At last he caught the elk of Hiisi, brought it to Pohjola and gave it to Louhi: 'I have done it; give me your daughter.' But Louhi set him a second task. In the poem these prayers run long, preserving the words with which old Finnish hunters asked the forest spirits for game; Tapio's realm, Tapiola, is a rich kingdom in the forest. This time Lemminkäinen succeeded not by boasting but by humble prayer.
sections.bodyZh: 勒明凯宁修好了滑雪板，这一次他不再夸口，而是向森林之神祈祷。他向森林之王塔皮奥和森林女主人米耶利基唱起祈祷的歌：森林的主人啊，美丽的森林之母啊，请打开你的金库，把那头麋鹿赶到我的路上来，我会用金子和银子报答你。他唱森林的美丽，唱森林之母穿着金色的衣裙，唱树木像盛装的人一样站立。他一连祈祷了三天，森林之神被他的歌声感动了，把那头麋鹿赶到了他面前。勒明凯宁终于捉住了希西的麋鹿，把它带回波赫约拉交给洛希，说：我已经做到了，把女儿给我吧。可是洛希又提出了第二个难题。在原诗里，这些祈祷占了很长的篇幅，保留了古代芬兰猎人向森林神灵祈求猎物的祷词；塔皮奥的国度叫塔皮奥拉，是森林中一个富足的王国。这一次，勒明凯宁靠的不是夸口，而是谦卑的祈求。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十四章。

sections.bodyEn: Louhi said: 'Go and bridle the brown gelding of Hiisi, which runs on Hiisi's meadows breathing fire from its nostrils and smoke from its mouth.' Lemminkäinen set out with a golden halter and a silver bridle. The horse came galloping, and the flames from its nostrils let no one near. Lemminkäinen prayed: 'Highest Ukko, send down hail and sleet on this wild horse and quench its fire.' Ukko sent down hail like iron, the fire on the horse was quenched, and Lemminkäinen stepped up and coaxed it gently: 'Good horse, do not harm me; bow your head into this golden halter. I will not strike you with the whip.' The horse bowed its head; he bridled it and rode back to Pohjola. Still Louhi would not give him her daughter, and named a third task, in a place far more terrible than the first two. Once again he succeeded not by force but by prayer and gentle words.
sections.bodyZh: 洛希说：你去把希西那匹棕色的骟马套上笼头，它在希西的原野上奔跑，鼻孔里喷着火，嘴里冒着烟。勒明凯宁带着金笼头和银马勒出发了。那匹马奔过来，鼻孔里喷出的火焰让人无法靠近。勒明凯宁向乌戈祈求：至高的乌戈啊，请降下冰雹和雪雨，落在这匹烈马的身上，浇灭它的火焰。乌戈降下了铁一样的冰雹，那匹马被冰雹浇灭了身上的火，勒明凯宁趁机走上前去，用温和的话哄它：好马啊，不要伤害我，低下你的头来，套上这金色的笼头吧，我不会用鞭子抽你。马低下了头，他给它套上了笼头，骑着它回到了波赫约拉。可洛希还是不肯把女儿给他，又说出了第三个难题，这一次的地方，比前两次都要可怕得多。这一次，他又一次学会了不靠蛮力，而是靠祈求和温和的话语。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十四章。

sections.bodyEn: Louhi said: 'Go to the black river of Tuonela, and with a single arrow shoot the swan there; then my daughter shall be yours.' Tuonela was the land of the dead, and the black river lay in the realm of Tuoni, lord of the dead. Lemminkäinen took his bow and arrows and went to the falls of the black river to wait for the swan. But the blind herdsman Märkähattu, whom he had mocked, lay in wait by the river. Seeing Lemminkäinen come, he drew a water-serpent from the river and hurled it like a spear; it passed under Lemminkäinen's left arm and through his heart and out at his right shoulder. Lemminkäinen fell and said in his agony: 'I was careless: I never asked my mother, never learned the charm against the water-serpent. I knew three charms but not this one. If my mother were here, she would tell me what to do.' The swan swimming on the river of the dead became a famous image in Finnish art; Sibelius's tone poem The Swan of Tuonela takes its subject from here.
sections.bodyZh: 洛希说：你去图奥内拉的黑河上，只射一箭，射死那里的天鹅，我就把女儿给你。图奥内拉是亡者之地，那条黑河就在亡者之王图奥尼的国度里。勒明凯宁背着弓箭，来到黑河边的瀑布旁，等着天鹅游过来。可是那个被他嘲笑过的盲眼牧人马尔卡哈图早就埋伏在河边了。他看见勒明凯宁走来，就从河水里抓起一条水蛇，像投矛一样投过去，水蛇穿过了勒明凯宁的左腋，刺穿了他的心脏和右肩。勒明凯宁倒在地上，痛苦地说：我真是疏忽啊，我没有问过母亲，没有学会对付水蛇的咒语。我知道三条咒语，却唯独不知道这一条。如果母亲在身边，她一定会告诉我该怎么办。这只在亡者之河上游动的天鹅，后来成了芬兰艺术中有名的形象，作曲家西贝柳斯的交响诗《图奥内拉的天鹅》就取材于此。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十四章。

sections.bodyEn: The blind herdsman threw the dying Lemminkäinen into the black river of Tuonela, and the current swept him towards the roaring falls. The son of Tuoni, lord of the dead — a man stained with blood — stood in the river with a knife, hewed Lemminkäinen into pieces and threw them into the deep waters of Tuonela, saying: 'Lie there with your bow and arrows, and shoot the swan on the river.' So the hero vanished into the depths of the river of the dead, with no grave, and no one knowing where he lay. Far away at home his mother and wife still waited for him. The rune is brief and dark; the singer tells Lemminkäinen's death in a few lines, as if the song itself would not linger by that black river. But in the Kalevala death is not always the end of the story. The poem calls him the bloody son of Tuoni. The swan still swam quietly on the black river; no one had shot it.
sections.bodyZh: 盲眼牧人把奄奄一息的勒明凯宁扔进了图奥内拉的黑河里，河水把他卷向汹涌的瀑布。亡者之王图奥尼的儿子——一个满身血污的人——站在河里，拿着刀把勒明凯宁砍成了好几块，扔进了图奥内拉深深的河水里，说：你就在这里躺着吧，带着你的弓和箭，去射河上的天鹅吧。一位英雄就这样消失在亡者之河的深处，没有坟墓，也没有人知道他的下落。远方的家中，母亲和妻子还在等着他回来。这一章短促而阴暗，诗人只用几句话就交代了勒明凯宁的死，仿佛连诗歌本身也不愿在这黑河边多停留一刻。可是在《卡勒瓦拉》里，死亡并不总是故事的终点。原诗把图奥尼的儿子称为“血红的图奥尼之子”。那只天鹅仍在黑河上静静地游着，没有人射中它。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十四章。
sections.headingEn: The pieces in the black river

sections.bodyEn: At home, Lemminkäinen's mother watched the brush every day. One day blood suddenly oozed from it. Weeping, she gathered up her skirts and ran all the way north. In Pohjola she demanded of Louhi: 'Where is my son?' Louhi said first that she had given him a horse, then that she had sent him hunting. 'You lie!' said the mother. 'Tell the truth, or I will destroy your storehouses and smash your Sampo.' Then Louhi admitted she had sent Lemminkäinen to shoot the swan of Tuonela. The mother searched everywhere. She asked the trees, and the trees said: 'We have troubles enough of our own; we have not seen your son.' She asked the road, and the road said: 'I am trodden and crushed by wheels; I have not seen him.' She asked the moon, and the moon did not know. At last she asked the sun, and the sun said: 'Your son is in the black river of Tuonela, hewn to pieces, lying at the bottom.' The sun, high in the sky, sees everything, and so it alone knew the truth. Hearing it, the mother stopped weeping and turned to find someone who could help her bring her son up from the river.
sections.bodyZh: 在勒明凯宁的家里，母亲每天都看着那把梳子。有一天，梳子上忽然渗出了血。母亲大哭起来，立刻提起裙子，一路奔向北方。她来到波赫约拉，逼问洛希：我的儿子在哪里？洛希先说给了他一匹马，又说让他去打猎了。母亲说：你在撒谎！快说实话，不然我就毁掉你的仓库，打碎你的三宝。洛希这才说出，她派勒明凯宁去射图奥内拉的天鹅。母亲到处寻找，她问树木，树木说：我们自己的苦已经够多了，没有看见你的儿子；她问道路，道路说：我被人踩、被车轧，没有看见；她问月亮，月亮也说不知道。最后她问太阳，太阳说：你的儿子在图奥内拉的黑河里，他被砍成了碎块，沉在河底。太阳高高在天上，什么都看得见，所以只有它知道真相。母亲听了，不再哭泣，而是转身去找能帮她把儿子捞上来的人。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十五章。

sections.bodyEn: Weeping, the mother went to the smith Ilmarinen and asked for a rake with copper teeth a hundred fathoms long and a handle five hundred fathoms long, and Ilmarinen forged it. At the black river of Tuonela she asked the sun to put the people of the land of the dead to sleep, then raked the river again and again. She raked up her son's shirt, his boots and his hat, and at last his body from the bottom — but a hand was missing, half the head and many bones. She raked again and again until she had found every piece. She laid the pieces together and called on Suonetar, goddess of the veins, to join the severed veins with her spindle, bone to bone and flesh to flesh. Still her son could not speak. So she sent a little bee for honey. The honey it gathered from the meadows did not help; what it brought from over the sea was not enough; at last it flew beyond the nine heavens and brought the Creator's own honey from his house. The mother anointed her son, and Lemminkäinen woke and said: 'How long I have slept!' When she asked why he still wanted to go to Pohjola, he said the maiden was waiting for him; she persuaded him to give it up and took him home.
sections.bodyZh: 母亲哭着去找铁匠伊尔马里宁，请他打一把耙子：铜的耙齿要一百寻长，耙柄要五百寻长。伊尔马里宁为她打好了铜耙。母亲来到图奥内拉的黑河边，请太阳让亡者之地的人们都睡去，然后用铜耙在河里一遍遍地耙，耙出了儿子的衬衫，耙出了他的靴子和帽子，最后在河底耙出了儿子的身体，可还少了一只手、半个头和许多块骨头。她又耙了一遍又一遍，终于把所有的碎块都找齐了。她把碎块拼在一起，请掌管血脉的女神苏奥内塔尔用纺锤把断开的血管一根根接起来，把骨头接上骨头，把肉接上肉。可儿子还是不能说话。母亲就派一只小蜜蜂去取蜜膏，蜜蜂先在草地上采来蜜，没有用；又飞过海去取，还是不够；最后飞过了九重天，从造物主的屋子里取来了神的蜜膏。母亲把蜜膏涂在儿子身上，勒明凯宁醒了过来，说：我睡得多么久啊。母亲问他为什么还想去波赫约拉，他说那个少女还在等他。母亲劝他放弃，带着他回到了家乡。
sections.evidenceNote: 《卡勒瓦拉》克劳福德译本第十五章。
